morningFacts: Light and darkness are the strongest environmental signals for the body's circadian clocks.
Nearly every tissue and organ has its own circadian rhythm; the brain keeps the tiny clock committee coordinated.
A brain region called the suprachiasmatic nucleus acts as the body's master clock and helps control melatonin using light cues.
Your sleep-wake cycle is shaped by both a circadian clock and sleep pressure that builds while you are awake.
Adenosine builds up in the brain during waking, and caffeine promotes alertness mainly by blocking its receptors.
Caffeine can start taking effect within about 15 to 45 minutes, though timing varies.
Caffeine's half-life is often five to six hours, so an afternoon cup can still be active near bedtime.
The grogginess and slower thinking after waking have a name: sleep inertia.
Morning civil twilight begins when the Sun's center is 6 degrees below the horizon.
Sunrise colors often look warm because low-angle sunlight travels through more atmosphere before reaching you.
The Sun only appears to rise; Earth's rotation carries you into sunlight, which is frankly dramatic enough.
Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees, which drives the seasons and shifts sunrise through the year.
At many mid-northern latitudes, the year's earliest sunrise happens before the summer solstice.
Dew forms when a surface cools below the dew point of the nearby air.
Roosters can begin crowing before sunrise because an internal circadian clock helps time the performance.
Sunrise and sunset on Mars can look blue near the Sun because fine dust scatters light differently there.
From Mars, the Sun appears only about two-thirds as wide as it does from Earth.
Martian twilight can last as long as two hours because high-altitude dust keeps scattering sunlight.
On Venus, the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east because Venus rotates backward compared with Earth.
Circadian rhythms repeat on a cycle of roughly 24 hours, even in organisms that never own a clipboard.
